shows.title: Works on Paper, 2000-2018
shows.description: The gallery's sixth exhibition of the South African artist William Kentridge brings together prints and a drawing made between 2000 and 2018. The works use linocut, pigment print, drypoint, etching, lithography and charcoal, and many are printed onto pages torn from old books such as early editions of the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary and the Encyclopaedia Britannica, so each print is unique.

shows.title: Coherence in Chaos
shows.description: Seattle artist Michael Schultheis, who has shown with the gallery for 20 years, presents new paintings, pastels and bronze sculptures built around the epicycloid, the curve traced as one circle rolls around another. One center stands for a person finding inner balance, two for a relationship, many for families and communities, and the works ask what holds us together.

shows.title: Look Upon This Body As A Machine
shows.description:
Ilana Zweschi's second solo show at Foster/White pushes further into the strange territory where mathematics and figuration meet. Zweschi, who studied both art and math at Skidmore before an MFA in painting at SUNY Albany, builds her large abstract canvases from handwritten algorithms that dictate the placement and gradation of individual brushstrokes — but underneath that procedural surface sit figurative drawings, giving the algorithm an organic body to work against.

The results are paintings that read as abstract from a distance and only slowly reveal the ghosted figure buried in their logic — bodies rendered as systems, as the show's title bluntly states. Zweschi has shown at Tiger Strikes Asteroid in New York and in the Out of Sight survey of Pacific Northwest art, and her work sits in the Microsoft and SeaTac collections; this show marks a continued deepening of a practice that treats painting as equal parts intuition and equation.

shows.title: As Seen In…
shows.description:
"As Seen In..." is J. Rinehart Gallery's chance to take a bow for a run of strong museum placements: it gathers gallery artists whose work has recently appeared in institutional shows around the country and puts that same work, or closely related pieces, on the gallery walls in Pioneer Square. Jaq Chartier, Katy Stone, and Emily Gherard all have pieces connected to "Women of the Pacific Northwest," a survey that traveled to the Bo Bartlett Center and the Asheville Art Museum; Cable Griffith's contribution relates to his Tacoma Art Museum exhibition "Uncanny Twilight"; and Priscilla Dobler Dzul shows work tied to her recent solo exhibition at the Frye Art Museum.

The result is a loosely thematic group show anchored by process-driven abstraction: Stone's layered cut-and-painted willow forms, Gherard's intaglio-and-plaster wall reliefs, Chartier's time-based chemical color studies, and Griffith's dyed and painted fabric compositions all approach observation and materials science from different angles, with an emphasis on unconventional or hybrid techniques.

It's a smart curatorial move — using museum validation as a lens for a commercial show — and a good one-stop introduction to several artists who've been quietly building serious institutional resumes without necessarily being household names yet in Seattle's gallery scene.

shows.title: Recent Work
shows.description:
Tucked into studio e's gallery annex, this focused presentation of new paintings by Bay Area artist Heather Wilcoxon runs alongside the main gallery's programming. Wilcoxon works from memory rather than observation, building canvases where strong, thick lines cut across colorful, atmospheric fields — a technique she's described as painting almost with her eyes closed, letting half-recognizable shapes surface from the subconscious.

The newer paintings on view continue the searching, oceanic quality of her longtime practice: forms that suggest familiar objects or bodies without ever fully resolving into them, so that looking becomes a kind of low-grade uncertainty rather than straightforward recognition. Wilcoxon has shown with studio e for over a decade, and this annex hang gives a compact, well-timed look at where her painting has moved since her last full show with the gallery.

It's a quieter complement to studio e's main-space program, worth a stop on its own for anyone who responds to moody, associative abstraction pitched somewhere between landscape and figure.

shows.title: Encore: Owls and Ravens – The Final Carvings
shows.description:
At 91, and after fifteen prior shows with Stonington Gallery, wood carver Hib Sabin is calling this one his last. The exhibition is built from his familiar bestiary — owls, ravens, shapeshifting guardians, small ritual vessels — carved from wood and often paired with the graphite studies that preceded them, so viewers can see a piece move from sketch to finished sculpture. Sabin has spent decades returning to the same handful of creatures as vehicles for thinking about aging, memory, and what gets carried forward, and that preoccupation feels especially direct here.

The carvings are small-scale and intimate rather than monumental, meant for close looking: weathered surfaces, deliberately worn textures, and animal faces that read as somewhere between totem and portrait. Because every major piece begins as a drawing, the show doubles as a look at Sabin's process, with works on paper offered alongside the sculptures they generated.

Billed as a final body of work rather than a retrospective, this is a chance to see a Pacific Northwest carving tradition — one Stonington has championed for years — brought to a deliberate close by one of its longtime practitioners. The opening falls on Pioneer Square's First Thursday art walk, with Sabin in attendance.

shows.title: In Celebration of Our 65th Anniversary: Masters of the Modern Northwest
shows.description:
Marking Woodside/Braseth's 65th year in business, this is a deep-bench survey of the painters who defined the mid-century "Northwest School" — Mark Tobey, Morris Graves, Guy Anderson, and Kenneth Callahan chief among them, joined by Paul Horiuchi's collage work and Louis Bunce. The gallery has pulled an unusually large run of works on paper alongside oils: Callahan's tempera and sumi-ink landscapes, Graves's tempera-on-gold bird studies, Tobey's ink and watercolor sketches of the old Pike Place Market, and Anderson's charcoal figure studies.

Because so much of the material is on paper and drawn from private holdings, this is a rarer chance to see the working, sketch-like side of artists usually represented by their signature large canvases — Tobey's small Pike Place Market studies from the early 1940s in particular offer a very different, more documentary view of the artist than his better-known abstract "white writing" paintings. Horiuchi's mixed-media collages, built from torn and layered paper, provide a textural counterpoint to the more painterly work around them.

Billed as being "in dialogue with" the mystically-inflected strain of Northwest painting these artists are known for, the show functions as much as a historical survey as a selling exhibition — a good primer for anyone trying to understand what critics meant by the "Northwest Mystics" label, and a chance to see significant works by these artists together in one gallery rather than scattered across museum collections.

shows.title: The Mother Road: 100 Years of Route 66
shows.description:
Kellie Talbot paints the roadside vernacular of mid-century America — motel marquees, diner signage, gas-station lettering — rendered in oil with a close, almost forensic attention to rust, chipped paint, and decades of weather damage. This show marks the 100th anniversary of Route 66 with a full set of new paintings built around the highway's iconic neon signs, each one a small portrait of a specific business and a specific stretch of road between Chicago and Los Angeles.

Talbot has said she's drawn to these signs for the combination of color, rust, and typography, and that the wear visible in her paintings functions as a kind of memento mori for the roadside culture the highway created. The paintings range from tight close-ups of individual letters and bulbs to wider views that place a sign back into its motel-and-parking-lot context, and the show includes a mix of small-format studies and larger canvases.

It's a straightforwardly nostalgic subject handled with real technical control, and a good example of the kind of accessible, collector-friendly painting show Patricia Rovzar Gallery has built its reputation on over more than three decades in downtown Seattle. The opening reception doubled as a Q&A with the artist about the project's year of research and travel along the historic route.

shows.title: The Holy Purry Order
shows.description:
Carles Gomila's Seattle solo debut through Roq La Rue is a small, dense cabinet of oil-on-panel paintings built around a single, strange conceit: the cat as sphinx, familiar, and stand-in for the divine feminine. Working from Menorca, largely self-taught, Gomila paints in a lush, symbolist register that borrows the gilded, saintly framing of 19th-century devotional painting and the pulpy exoticism of mid-century illustration, then points all of it at the everyday intimacy between women and their cats.

Each panel restages a familiar art-historical type — a Madonna, a martyr, an idol — with a cat standing in for (or alongside) the female figure, so that reverence and camp sit uneasily together. Titles like "Our Lady of Terms and Conditions" and "Know Your Enemy" signal the show's wit, but the paintings themselves are sincere: richly glazed, framed like relics, and clearly made by someone who has spent real time looking at the psychology of cats as much as at painting history.

It's a tightly focused body of work — eighteen-by-twenty-four-inch panels in matching black-and-gold frames — and most of the pieces had already sold by the show's final week, which says something about how well this register of pop-surrealist devotion has landed with Roq La Rue's audience. Worth a look for anyone interested in the gallery's long-running lowbrow/pop-surrealist lane, and for anyone who has ever tried to reconcile loving a creature that mostly tolerates you.

shows.title: Edges of Unmaking
shows.description:
Daphne Minkoff paints Seattle's disappearing built environment — boarded-up houses, aging storefronts, abandoned cars — but this isn't straightforward documentary work. Her mixed-media collage paintings tear and layer old photographs into the physical structure of each piece, so the surface itself carries the same sense of accumulation and decay as the subjects depicted. Titles like "Dead End," "Vacancies," and "The Past Is Never Dead" point to the show's real subject: what persists in memory after a place is gone.

Many of the specific buildings Minkoff painted have already been demolished and replaced by condos and mixed-use development, which gives the work an odd double life — it's part elegy, part evidence. The largest canvas here, "Between Grief and Nothing" at 60 x 50 inches, anchors a group of smaller, more intimate collage-paintings that read almost like relics pulled from a demolition site.

Minkoff has been showing variations on this theme at Harris Harvey for years (an earlier iteration, Façades, covered similar ground), and this new body of work sharpens the focus on transformation and loss rather than just the buildings themselves. It's a quiet, materially rich show about what a city forgets when it rebuilds itself, and worth a slow look given how much is packed into the torn-paper surfaces.

shows.title: What's the Story? Contemporary Narratives of Home, Identity and Connection
shows.artist: Al-Baseer Holly, Eric Chan, Lauren Iida, Periko the Artist, Samantha Yun Wall, and Vincent Keele
shows.description:
Six Pacific Northwest artists use the human figure as a vehicle for personal and collective memory in this group show at ArtX Contemporary. Eric Chan's densely worked oil paintings on reclaimed wood braid together classical Western painting, Asian pictorial traditions, and queer and immigrant experience into a kind of invented folklore. Al-Baseer Holly builds his canvases from collaged photographs of himself and his family, fusing painting and personal archive. Lauren Iida's hand-cut paper works, built from washes of ink and negative space, extend her ongoing engagement with her family's Japanese American incarceration history into present-day social and political territory.

The show also includes Vincent Keele's saturated history paintings, which recover overlooked or invented figures from Black history, Gerardo Peña's (Periko the Artist) surreal, dissonance-charged scenes of migration and unbelonging, and drawings by Samantha Yun Wall, whose SAM Betty Bowen Award show is running concurrently across town. Read together, the works trade the single-artist survey for a chorus of first-person accounts of home, inheritance, and displacement.

It's a strong entry point into ArtX Contemporary's long-running focus on cross-cultural exchange, gathering artists working in wildly different materials — oil, cut paper, collage, graphite — around a shared interest in what it means to picture where you come from. A Story Time artist talk on September 12 brings several of the participating artists together in conversation.

shows.title: Self. Reflexive.
shows.artist: Ian Brownlee, Gegam Kacherian, Michael Lazarus, Kaoru Mansour
shows.description:
Self. Reflexive. gathers four painters and drawers whose work turns inward, using the figure and everyday objects as vessels for private experience. Ian Brownlee's large, autobiographical oil paintings stage specific memories — a birthday, a father's funeral — with just enough distance and symbolism that they read as shared human stories rather than diary entries. Kaoru Mansour's obsessively worked colored-pencil drawings on paper and wood panel push in the opposite direction, building tightly rendered, slightly uncanny psychological portraits out of pattern and repetition.

Gegam Kacherian's acrylic paintings supply the show's more abstract register: geometric fields and cosmic imagery (a recurring interest in his work since his years in Los Angeles) that read as maps of interior states rather than places. Michael Lazarus contributes a deadpan series of small, single-object paintings of chairs, each one a stand-in for a body or a mood, rendered with the flat clarity of a still life. Brownlee also built an interactive painting installation for the gallery's front room, inviting visitors to add their own narrative to the work on view.

Together the four practices make a loose argument that self-portraiture doesn't require a face — it can be a chair, a pattern, a swirl of color, or a remembered room. It's a quiet, drawing-and-painting-forward show, well suited to AMcE's intimate gallery space on Capitol Hill.

shows.title: I Have Eyes for You
shows.artist: Mary Anne Carter, Trisha Gilmore, Aimee Hagedorn, Sonja Peterson, Erika Rier, and Paige Wright
shows.description:
Running in AMcE's Niche Market storefront alongside the main gallery's Self. Reflexive., I Have Eyes for You is a playful, craft-forward group show built around a single motif: the eye. Mary Anne Carter, working with Wishbone Industrial Arts, contributes hand-cut and slumped glass tableware — plates, coasters, and trinket dishes — printed with eyes in a way that turns a dinner table into a small game of being watched. Other contributors work the same theme through embroidery, tufting, and ceramics, giving the show a lively mix of textures and materials rather than a single dominant medium.

The premise is light on its feet, closer to a design showcase than a gallery statement show, and it fits the storefront's function as AMcE's rotating venue for functional and wearable art. It's a good stop for anyone looking for a distinctive, handmade gift or object as much as for viewers interested in how far a simple visual joke — eyes on everything — can be stretched across different craft traditions.

shows.title: IN | ROTATION
shows.description:
Hannah Delaney's paintings for IN | ROTATION read like liner notes rendered as portraiture — a run of canvases built around the musicians who have stayed in her personal rotation as she moved from Atlanta to London and now Belltown. Rather than straightforward likenesses, the work leans on saturated color and flattened, poster-like composition to capture the feeling of a song more than the appearance of the person singing it, which keeps the paintings closer to concert-poster energy than fan art.

The show is split into two halves at Slip: the paintings proper, and a companion pop-up shop of posters, hand-painted jackets, bags, and other wearable work made by local women artists, with all proceeds returning to the makers. That pairing is very much in keeping with Slip's model as a community storefront gallery — the art and the marketplace share the same room rather than being kept separate.

It's a modest, high-energy show best experienced on a Belltown Art Walk night, when Delaney has also been doing live painting sessions alongside the exhibition.

shows.title: The Things We Call Things
shows.description:
Two Seattle-area artists who each came up through construction trades turn scrap material into sculpture in this two-person show. Bill Grader builds towers, stacks and wall-mounted assemblages from stained wood and painted scrap plastic — modular, brightly colored forms that read like architectural models built from salvage. Andy McConnell works in a similarly transformed vocabulary of found material, using scribing and carving techniques picked up on job sites to turn cast-off wood and steel into abstract, gestural pieces with titles like "Relic" and "Gradient Cycle."

What unites the two bodies of work is less a shared palette than a shared instinct: both artists treat construction debris — trim scraps, counter slab offcuts, blackened steel — as raw material with its own history, worth preserving rather than discarding. The result is a show about second lives for objects, built by two people who spent careers giving buildings their first ones.

It's a modest, unpretentious survey of outsider-adjacent sculpture that rewards a slow look at surface and joinery — the kind of show where knowing a maker's background changes how you read the work.

shows.title: Unwavering Hope: 18th Annual Juried Exhibit
shows.artist: John Affolter, Deb Choat, Jo Cosme, Elizabeth Costello, Claudia Kimberly Crayton, Whitney Diggs, Malialani Dullanty, Carol Eaton, Brooke Gassiot, Deirdre Herron, Amuri Morris, Gabriela Nirino, Jelisa Peterson, Gary Rubin, Randall Steinke, James Thatcher, Li Turner
shows.description:
Columbia City Gallery's annual juried exhibition returns for its 18th edition, this year built around the theme of hope as an active, sustained practice rather than a passive feeling. Jurors James Coley (King Street Station Program Lead, Seattle Office of Arts & Culture) and gallerist Avery Barnes selected the seventeen participating artists from a national pool of more than 350 submissions, so the show functions as a snapshot of how a wide swath of working artists are answering a shared prompt.

Given the loose, single-word premise, expect real range: portraiture that leans into quiet resolve or open laughter, textile and weaving work, and pattern-based pieces that use repetition as a stand-in for endurance. The curatorial framing — drawn from remarks by Auburn poet laureate Mateo Quispe about hope as "a matter of attention" — pushes the work toward political and personal registers at once, asking what it looks like to keep paying attention to what sustains us during hard stretches.

As a juried show rather than a single-artist presentation, this is less about a unified visual argument than about breadth: seventeen distinct voices circling one idea from very different angles, media, and life experience. It's a good entry point if you want a cross-section of what's being made across the country right now under one loosely shared theme, in the intimate storefront setting of this Columbia City co-op gallery.

shows.title: Korean Rhapsody: Sijo at Gallery B612
shows.artist: MiYoung Margolis, KyoungMug Park, YoungHwa Choi
shows.description:
Three Korean-American artists build an exhibition around sijo, the concise three-line poetic form that dates to the late Goryeo Dynasty. Sijo's compressed structure — tension, expansion, resolution — becomes the curatorial logic here, with each work meant to echo that internal rhythm rather than illustrate a poem directly.

MiYoung Margolis, KyoungMug Park, and YoungHwa Choi work in ink, hanji (traditional Korean mulberry paper), and mixed media, translating calligraphic discipline and Korean literary tradition into a contemporary visual language. The show runs as a companion to a presentation the gallery staged during Korean Cultural Week at the Seattle Art Fair, and it's accompanied by live painting and dance performances and an ink brush workshop with Choi — a program that treats the exhibition as one part of a broader cultural exchange rather than a self-contained object show.

shows.title: The Kondō Family: Storytellers in Clay
shows.artist: Kondō Yūzō, Kondō Yutaka, Kondō Hiroshi, Kondō Takahiro
shows.description:
About sixty porcelain works by four artists across three generations of one of Japan's most influential ceramic families: Kondō Yūzō (1902-1985), named a Living National Treasure in 1977, his sons Kondō Yutaka and Kondō Hiroshi, and Hiroshi's son Kondō Takahiro (born 1958). Their work grows from sometsuke, cobalt blue painted under a clear glaze, which each generation took in new directions, up to Takahiro's 'Silver Mist' glazes, cast self-portrait heads and marbleized figures.

The works come from the Carol and Jeffrey Horvitz Collection. Organized by SAM, the show is based on Transcendent Clay/Kondo, first presented by the Lowe Art Museum, University of Miami, and guest curated by Joe Earle. Several images come from the museum's press kit and are small.

shows.title: Discontinuity
shows.description:
French sculptor Gabrielle Wambaugh works almost entirely in stoneware and porcelain, but treats the material as something to obscure rather than showcase — her pieces are built through layering, concealment, and partial reveal, so that a form's full shape is never quite visible from any single angle. That approach carries directly into this show's title: "Discontinuity" gathers sculptures where surface, glaze, and structure seem to interrupt each other mid-thought, gold luster breaking across cracked or ruptured stoneware forms that look simultaneously ancient and freshly damaged.

Wambaugh's practice runs through some of the most serious ceramics research institutions in Europe, including multiple residencies at the European Ceramic Workcentre in the Netherlands and research time at the Sèvres national porcelain manufactory in France, and that technical depth shows in the way these pieces handle glaze as a kind of skin — fused, crazed, or gilded rather than simply applied.

This marks Wambaugh's exhibition debut at Traver Gallery's West Canal Yards space, and it's a good excuse to see the gallery's striking new home on the Ship Canal at the north edge of Queen Anne, in a former fish-processing building reworked into one of the city's more dramatic exhibition spaces.

Based on the promotional image, expect figurative, dreamlike imagery built around the title's central symbol. shows.title: Light and Horizon
shows.description:
Marci Carlson's September show at Fogue turns entirely on the sky at its most dramatic hinge points — sunrise and sunset — rendered as a series of landscape studies gathered from locations around the world. The premise is simple and the execution is the point: how the same brief window of shifting light can transform an ordinary horizon line into something that reads as extraordinary, painting after painting.

As a single-artist survey built around one recurring subject, the show rewards being seen as a group rather than picking out individual pieces — the cumulative effect of repeated horizons in different palettes, from warm oranges and purples to cooler dawn tones, is where the work's argument about light and perception really lands. It's a straightforward, atmospheric show, well suited to Fogue's ongoing mission of spotlighting Pacific Northwest artists working past the emerging-artist stage of their careers.

Jacqui Beck paints everyday people and places, Barb Flye builds mosaics about migration and belonging, and Tara McDermott works across encaustic, painting and woodworking.

shows.title: Timeless Euphoria
shows.description: A community show by Trans and Two-Spirit artists of Black, Mexican, Chamorro, Puerto Rican and First Nations heritage: Kaotic Artz, Jay Robles (Mo'moy Creates), Amado Mar, Mar Olivos, Risåki Diego and Vaquero Azul. Through illustration, painting, mixed media, wearable art and storytelling, they picture worlds where authenticity and community are celebrated, with art as medicine and resistance.

shows.title: TALES UNWRITTEN
shows.description:
Drew Dyrdahl, a CORE member artist who builds work from cast-off materials, shows a set of handmade journals. Each is bound in leather, fabric and metal, and the paper signatures, of handmade paper from India and watercolor paper, are stitched by hand.

The gallery has posted one image of the journals; the second photo is one of Dyrdahl's earlier Little Creepers assemblages (salvaged boxes and stitched figures made from recycled clothing), from his CORE artist page.

shows.title: DECONSTRUCTION
shows.description:
Seattle photographer Michelle Smith-Lewis works with historic processes such as wet plate collodion and cyanotype. In Deconstruction she cuts apart cyanotypes printed on fabric and puts them back together as hanging panels, chains and new shapes.

The gallery has posted only an installation view (last photo). The other images are earlier cyanotypes by the artist from her own portfolio, leaf and flower prints that show the process the new work starts from.

shows.title: Pattern Recognition
shows.description: Pattern Recognition pairs aquatint etchings by printmaker Azumi Takeda with glass by guest artist Jason Christian, a glassblower rooted in the Pacific Northwest. Takeda's prints use aquatint, an intaglio technique that builds soft, wash-like tones rather than hard lines, often combined with etching; her quiet, patterned figures appear in series such as Floating Person, the Room prints and the Cometh prints.

shows.title: Please Touch: Breaking Barriers
shows.description: A tactile group show in Georgetown made to be touched, designed especially for blind and low-vision visitors. It includes textile, ceramic, basketry, cast and relief works by Lamar Van Dyke, Lucy and Pieter Van Zanden, Nancy Stokley, Sue Springer, Kathy Ross, Tina Ostrander, Louise Roby, Patti O, Colleen Monette, Jim Maris and Margaret MacLean.

shows.title: Warp, Weft and Landlines
shows.description: New paintings by Allison Collins, known for abstract landscapes drawn from the Pacific Northwest and Eastern Washington that are often called quilted landscapes, after rag rugs, Gee's Bend and Amish quilts. After seeing MoMA's exhibition on textiles and modern abstraction, she began weaving verticals and horizontals together with sweeping land lines, layering warm and cool color, texture and scratched lines into patchwork fields.

shows.title: Frye Parlor x Jayme Yen
shows.description: Frye Parlor is an artist-designed lounge that doubles as an experimental installation, spreading through the common areas between the auditorium, café and art studio. Its first version, by Jayme Yen, takes cues from Frye Salon, mixing painting, design and language through poetic phrases printed on fabric, reflective surfaces and fields of color. A new artist will redesign the space every two years.

shows.title: Boren Banner Series: Blake Blanco
shows.description:
Seattle artist Blake Blanco's 16 x 20 ft banner on the Frye's Boren Avenue facade reproduces a new oil painting, All that gleams against the tides (2026). Blanco sketches in a virtual reality studio and then paints the results, here drawing on a 1543 Italian engraving of Danaë and the infant Perseus cast out to sea, rendered in simplified shapes and bright synthetic colors. The banner series shows Pacific Northwest artists at billboard scale; it was organized by curatorial assistant Alexis L. Silva and is visible outdoors even when the galleries are closed.

The first image is the banner painting; the museum has posted no other images, so the rest are recent paintings by the artist from his own website.
shows.reception: Fall 2026 Public Exhibitions Reception, Friday, November 6, 2026

shows.title: My Body Is a Basket
shows.artist: Brenda Mallory, Danielle Morsette, Sara Siestreem
shows.description: A three-artist show of Indigenous artists based in Washington and Oregon who push textile traditions in new directions: Brenda Mallory (Cherokee Nation), Danielle Morsette and Sara Siestreem (Hanis Coos). Across sculpture, wool weaving and mixed-media painting, basketry works as both method and metaphor. It was conceived alongside the touring An Indigenous Present and is co-curated by Faith Brower and Asia Tail.
shows.reception: Fall 2026 Public Exhibitions Reception, Friday, November 6, 2026; artist conversation Saturday, November 7

shows.title: An Indigenous Present
shows.description: A touring exhibition organized by the Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston with groupings of work by fifteen Indigenous artists who use abstraction to tell personal and collective stories and to build on cultural traditions. It is co-curated by artist Jeffrey Gibson and Jenelle Porter, growing out of their 2023 book of the same name, and spans elders and emerging makers including Teresa Baker, Raven Chacon, Sky Hopinka, George Morrison, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith and Kay WalkingStick.

shows.title: Stefan Gonzales: Field Research
shows.description: The first solo museum show for Seattle artist Stefan Gonzales, who studies overlooked industrial materials taken from the land. Field Research focuses on rock salt used to de-ice roads, through sculpture, photographs, archival cabinets and a film that track how the salt dissolves and recrystallizes in water. The work also looks back at Minimalism and Land art and ties the material to questions of labor and resource extraction.

shows.title: Recent Acquisitions
shows.description: Timed to the Frye's 75th anniversary, this show presents works added to the collection during 2025-26, one of its biggest periods of growth. It mixes Pacific Northwest and other artists, many new to the collection, from Vik Muniz and Marie Watt to Kenneth Callahan and Morris Graves. A carved cedar sculpture by Ursula von Rydingsvard, on extended loan, anchors a section with works by Guy Anderson, Paul Horiuchi, Hugh Hayden, Koak and Robyn O'Neil.

shows.title: Nicole Eisenman | Esther Hamerman: Life After Life
shows.description: The first major survey of Esther Hamerman, a self-taught painter and Jewish refugee from Nazi Europe who began painting in her sixties in New York, organized with her great-grandchild, the painter Nicole Eisenman. Nearly all of Hamerman's known work hangs with a selection of Eisenman's paintings from the last twenty years. The pairing is about emotional kinship more than influence: two generations picturing memory, community and shared life.

shows.title: Boren Banner Series: Serrah Russell
shows.description:
For the Frye's seventy-fifth anniversary, the museum opened its archives to the Seattle artist Serrah Russell, known for hand-cut photo collages that find new relationships among existing images. Working by hand, she is layering records of the institution and of its founders, Charles and Emma Frye, including their business and family papers, into a new photomontage that holds poetic association and social critique in the same frame.

The work will be shown as a 16 x 20 ft vinyl banner on the museum's east facade on Boren Avenue, part of the Boren Banner Series of work by Pacific Northwest artists. Organized by Alexis L. Silva, Curatorial Assistant. The first image is Russell's collage towards empathy (2015), shown on the Frye's page; the others show recent work by the artist, as the new banner has not been published yet.

shows.title: Under the Sky
shows.description: A show about the sky in art, mainly European and American work from 1870 to 1920. Landscape paintings from the Frye's Founding Collection hang with photographs of the same era from the Maren Monsen and Jeff Grainger Collection, showing how artists after the Industrial Revolution looked outward and upward to explore spirituality and regional and national identity.

shows.title: Here & Now
shows.description: A selection of paintings, photographs, prints, sculpture and mixed-media works recently bought for the King County Public Art Collection through 4Culture's Here and Now open call, its first direct purchase of portable art in nearly a decade. A peer panel chose 165 works by 123 artists from across the region; after the show the pieces will rotate through county buildings such as clinics, courthouses and community centers. Last day is October 16.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 3, 6-8pm; second reception Thursday, October 1, 6-8pm

venue.address: 101 Prefontaine Pl S, Seattle, WA 98104, USA

shows.title: Pythia Embodied
shows.description:
Afroditi Psarra, a Seattle artist who teaches in the University of Washington's DXARTS program, presents Pythia Embodied: an AI oracle that runs on a wearable device on the body rather than in the cloud, trained on texts about magic, ritual, secret ceremonies and ancient myth. Through spoken voices, interactions and textile offerings, the piece raises questions about technological control of the female body. Receptions are November 5 and December 3.

4Culture has not posted images from the show yet; shown here are recent works by the artist. They include Ventriloquist Ontology (2022), a talking wearable trained on texts about the body and gender, and knitted tapestries from her sound installation Altar. The show was chosen for 4Culture's 2026-27 season by Diana Falchuk, Jordan Jones and Allyce Wood.

shows.title: Eight x Eight Annual
shows.description: The gallery's annual small-works show, in which every piece measures 8 by 8 inches. Around two dozen emerging and established artists, including Lisa Alden, Andrea Brice, MiYoung Margolis, Ellen Ramsey and Travis Thurber, show work across many styles and subjects, sized for gifting.

shows.title: Vibrant Palette Arts Center: Fantastical Collaborational Invitational
shows.description: Vibrant Palette Arts Center, a studio for artists with autism and intellectual and developmental disabilities, shows its artists alongside the Greenwood Art Collective and guest artists including Jorge Cainas, Xin Lu and Anastasia Rudenco. The show hangs the work side by side on equal footing, answering the way such artists have often been set apart from their local art scenes. Twenty-seven artists take part.

shows.title: Happily Ever After
shows.description: A group show about fairy tales and folklore from around the world, with seventeen artists including EVAN, Katja Bakker, Lezlie Jane, Sofia Krasnovskaya and Usako Nan. Some make new pictures that echo familiar stories; others look for wonder and whimsy in everyday life. It was planned alongside the O-Jak Bridge Art and Dance Festival's dance production Once Upon a Time.

shows.title: Geometry of Memory: New Works by Cathie Joy Young
shows.description: Painter Cathie Joy Young shows acrylic paintings on wood panel where history, nature and technology meet. She builds saturated, organic surfaces from layered glazes and washes, then uses fine brushwork to tell symbolic stories about information overload and the friction between truth and belief.

shows.title: Dance with Color
shows.description: London-born artist Shima Star celebrates unity across cultures through a cycle of painting, photography, digital transformation, printing, collage and gestural mark-making. Inspired by Matisse's The Dance, her bright paintings feature the Star People, archetypal figures drawn from myth and celestial imagery, alone in the Lone Star series and finally joined in a cosmic dance in the title work.
shows.reception: First Thursday, October 1, 5-8pm; reception and artist talk Saturday, October 24, 4-6pm; meet & greet Saturday, October 31, 12-4pm

shows.title: Intwined
shows.description: Rebecca Woodhouse cuts apart her own linoprints and weaves them with vintage neckties, many from the closets of a friend's father, a WWII survivor who collected them for decades, into collages about memory and generational bonds. Shown with her richly layered linocut paintings, the work mixes traditionally masculine and feminine materials to question Modernism's gendered legacy.
shows.reception: First Thursday, October 1, 5-8pm; reception and artist talk Saturday, October 24, 4-6pm

shows.title: Healing From Nature and Discovering Her Sculptural Materials
shows.description:
Sculpture and assemblage by Seattle artist Kathy Bussert-Webb made from humble and organic materials: branches, thrifted objects, natural pigments, paper pulp and sewn sheets of dried kombucha SCOBY, a material she has researched and written about. Birds recur as stand-ins for the artist, and several pieces are lit from behind on lightboxes.

Drawing on Arte Povera and eco-art, the works deal with loss, trauma and recovery, with nature cast as witness and healer. Works shown here include Peaceful Impermanence, Light amid Loss, Moonlight Stroll and Cycle (all 2026), from the artist's current body of work; the gallery page itself posts only the first.
shows.reception: First Thursday, October 1, 5-8pm; reception and artist talk Saturday, October 24, 4-6pm

shows.title: Reclaimed : Renewed
shows.description:
Marcus Lelle takes the cyanotype, the blue sun-printing process usually seen on paper, off the wall and into clothing and objects. The nine pieces fall into three groups: a patchwork vest and skirt sewn from thrifted denim and a cargo jacket, a jacket built from 152 small cyanotypes printed on a bedsheet and paired with filmstrip-printed jeans, and an electric guitar dyed with cyanotype chemistry.

A set of conventional wall prints of Seattle scenes (Post Alley, an aerial view of downtown, the Edmonds rail line) rounds out the show as a counterpoint. Lelle, who identifies as non-binary, frames the wearable pieces around slow, sustainable making with reclaimed materials and clothing that fits outside gender norms.
shows.reception: First Thursday, November 5, 5-8pm; artist reception Saturday, November 7, 4-6pm

shows.title: Radiant Echoes
shows.description:
Matthew Behrend shows new "electric patina" works, a process he invented in which he shapes electric fields in a water bath so that they print colored forms into brass and copper plates. Each piece starts from an image seen in meditation; the iridescent surfaces shift in color as the viewer moves.

Behrend trained as an electrical engineer and did his doctoral research on the neural interface of the first FDA-approved retinal implant. The show includes works such as Nirvana Rebirth (2026, brass, 18 x 24 in.).
shows.reception: First Thursday, November 5, 5-8pm; artist reception Saturday, November 7, 4-6pm

shows.title: Spectacle of Being
shows.description:
Oil paintings by Washington painter Sarah Barnett that treat the operating theater as a stage where the exposed body, surgical equipment, screens and onlookers come together. The title work, Spectacle of Being (2026), is a 60 x 72 inch canvas.

Barnett, whose earlier In Vivo series also drew on anatomy and medical machinery, uses close-up, distorted views to look at how technologies once imagined in fiction are becoming part of the body and everyday life.
shows.reception: First Thursday, November 5, 5-8pm; artist reception Saturday, November 7, 4-6pm

shows.title: Please Touch: Together, Breaking Barriers
shows.description: A group show of art made to be touched, especially welcoming to visitors who are blind, deafblind or have low vision, and inviting sighted visitors to experience art beyond looking. Please Touch has moved between Seattle venues for ten years. This October it is shown at both Gray Sky Gallery and Fogue Studios in Georgetown to raise awareness of accessibility in the arts.

shows.title: The Visible and The Vanishing
shows.description: Darrell Peterson shows encaustic paintings of flowers that seem to appear and fade at once. He builds thick, textured surfaces from layered molten beeswax, damar resin and pigment, so botanical forms rise out of and sink back into translucent wax.

shows.title: Crossroads
shows.description: Gallery owner Laura Van Horne and ceramicist Karen Abel take the Swiss cross as a shared symbol of turning points and life choices. Van Horne's layered mixed-media works are paired with Abel's richly textured ceramics.

shows.title: Peaceful Journey
shows.description: Magdalena Cooney shows large acrylic paintings. The gallery has posted few details so far.
shows.dates_note: Listed Dec 2 - Dec 30, 2026, but the text gives the opening reception as Thursday, January 7.

shows.title: Drawings On Wood
shows.description: John Buck's eighth solo show at the gallery is thirteen ink drawings on panels of jelutong, the pale, soft wood he has used for decades in his sculptures and woodblock prints. Drawn in ballpoint pen, the images of rock and water formations, mountains and desert of the American West are drawn from turn-of-the-century engravings in old books from the artist's collection.
shows.reception: Thursday, November 5, 6-8pm (artist attending); also Thursday, December 3, 6-8pm

shows.title: My Labors
shows.description: The gallery's twelfth solo exhibition of sculpture by Seattle artist Ed Wicklander, who works in carved wood, welded and cast metal, silver soldering, electroforming and mold making. The pieces mix folk tradition with invention: a dreamlike take on Henry Fuseli's painting The Nightmare, a portrait of one of his cats stretching, and a tiny pair of cast-iron briefs on a hanger.
shows.reception: Thursday, November 5, 6-8pm (artist attending); also Thursday, December 3, 6-8pm; artist talk Saturday, November 7 at noon

shows.title: Poems of the Earth
shows.description: Pacific Northwest painter Hart James makes bold abstractions in oil and charcoal that call up moving water, air and stone. Working in the tradition of the Northwest Mystics, she treats each painting as a way back into a close relationship with the natural world. The show is paired with Gregg Laananen's Fire in the Moon.

shows.title: Fire in the Moon
shows.description: Gregg Laananen is a self-taught painter who lives and works in the Skagit Valley. His thickly worked paintings, made both in the studio and outdoors, show Northwest waterfalls, forests and rocky coast alongside floral still lifes, in a direct, expressive style. The show runs alongside Hart James's Poems of the Earth.

shows.title: Distant Visions
shows.description: Linda Jo Nazarenus paints detailed landscapes and wildlife in thin layered oil glazes, a method drawn from Northern Renaissance painting. In Distant Visions her animals share the frame with human markers of longing and belief, such as the Very Large Array's dishes, the Trinity Site obelisk, a lone church and the Space Needle, drawn from Sweden and the American Southwest.

shows.title: “Every Picture Somewhat of an Experiment”: Helen Frankenthaler Prints
shows.description: The first showing of a 2023 gift of prints and proofs from the Helen Frankenthaler Foundation's Prints Initiative. From 1961 into the 2000s the Abstract Expressionist painter made more than 300 print editions in etching, lithography, screenprint and woodcut with workshops such as ULAE, Tyler Graphics and Garner Tullis, and the show follows that whole arc. Two recent works by Los Angeles artist Analia Saban carry her experiments into the present.

shows.title: Day-to-Day: Rhythm, Routine, Resistance
shows.description:
A group show in the Lower Level Gallery, drawn mostly from the Henry's collection with a few loans from regional private collections, about the poetics and politics of everyday life. Works from roughly the last thirty years by U.S.-based artists turn ordinary objects, routines and rooms into places to think about labor, belonging and the forces that shape daily life: Rashid Johnson's film of his family's routines, Dawn Clements' panoramic drawing of a temporary home, and Tony Feher's hanging rope of plastic bottles among them.

The 25 artists include Nayland Blake, Andrea Bowers, Tara Donovan, Genevieve Gaignard, Jenny Holzer, Jessica Jackson Hutchins, Larry Mantello, Louise Nevelson, Ruben Ochoa, Liliana Porter, Amanda Ross-Ho, Mickalene Thomas and Dan Webb. It was organized by senior curator Nina Bozicnik with Em Chan.

shows.title: Viewpoints: Shark by Richard Learoyd
shows.description: A one-work presentation in the Henry's Viewpoints series, which pairs a collection piece with responses from the University of Washington community. Richard Learoyd's Shark (2009) is a large, grainless unique print of a dead grey reef shark, made with a room-sized camera obscura he built himself. Writers from art history, anthropology and marine biology reflect on how it draws on scientific photography, still life and histories of extraction.

shows.title: Joiri Minaya: To Hell with Hibiscus
shows.description: New York-born, Dominican Republic-raised artist Joiri Minaya looks at 'the Tropics' as an invented place and identity. In the Henry's double-height gallery she shows the textile language she has built to critique it, from altered Aloha shirts to the floral spandex she designed to cloak colonial monuments, using Seattle as a link to shared histories across the Global South. The installation plays with hiding and revealing.

shows.title: screen-skin field: Seattle (Henry Art Gallery)
shows.description: A new mural for the Henry's exterior facade by New York artist Tishan Hsu, who since the 1980s has explored how technology shapes the body. Growing out of his recent wallpaper works, it blends skin-like textures, warped grids and grass-sprouting openings into a surface between the organic and the digital. Being outdoors, it can be seen any time.
shows.dates_note: Page gives 'August 2026 – January 2028' (no days); start/end set to month bounds.

shows.title: Charlene Liu: Scallion
shows.description:
Charlene Liu, an artist based in Eugene, Oregon, who was born in Taiwan and raised in the Midwest, made the first mural for the Henry's Sculpture Court. Scallion (2025), an inkjet print on vinyl, is a dense imagined landscape built from food-inspired forms in bands of saturated color.

The mural continues Liu's use of food as a way into culture and heritage in diaspora, celebrating shared meals and how culinary traditions build a sense of belonging. It is on view through July 2027. The Henry's site currently notes that the Sculpture Court is temporarily closed for maintenance.
shows.dates_note: July 2025 - July 2027

shows.title: Invention into Existence
shows.description:
A large group show of nearly 20 artists and 30 works, including new commissions, on hopes and fears about technologies reshaping how we sense and live in the world. Its title comes from Frantz Fanon's call for 'introducing invention into existence', and it is arranged in three clusters: systems of knowledge, bodies as technological assemblages, and resource extraction.

Many of the emerging and mid-career artists are making their Pacific Northwest debut: Morehshin Allahyari, American Artist, Stephanie Dinkins, Jes Fan, Matthew Angelo Harrison, Tishan Hsu, Maya Jeffereis, Kite, Amor Muñoz, Rashaad Newsome, Berenice Olmedo, Mimi Ọnụọha, Sondra Perry, Sarah Rosalena, Bogosi Sekhukhuni, Stephanie Syjuco and Paul Vanouse. It is one of the Henry's two centennial-year exhibitions, organized by associate curator Swagato Chakravorty.
shows.dates_note: Opens February 20, 2027; closes February 2028

shows.title: The Henry Collection At 100
shows.description: For its centennial (it opened in 1927 as Washington's first public art museum), the Henry fills its original 1927 building with focused selections from a collection that has grown from 172 to nearly 30,000 works. Groupings look at representation, national myths, image economies, exchange between cultures, technology, and queer and feminist embodiment. Anchors include Winslow Homer's An Adirondack Lake (1870) with 19th-century landscape photographs, and Rauschenberg's Booster beside early video by Seattle's Doris Totten Chase.
shows.dates_note: Page gives 'February 20, 2027 - August 2027'; end set to 2027-08-31.

shows.title: Amir H. Fallah: A Declaration
shows.description: The first commission in a new series for the Henry's three-story central stairwell. Los Angeles artist Amir H. Fallah, born in Tehran, will wrap the stairwell in a mural collaged from his archive of images and add sculptural tableaux with video collages in which people silently mouth 'I am an American', a portrait of American identity in its contradictions.
shows.dates_note: Page says only 'Opening February 20, 2027'; no end date given.

shows.title: Lunacy
shows.description: The gallery's second solo show with Tacoma-raised illustrator, painter and muralist Kelly Bjork. Lunacy is a set of intimate scenes in gouache, watercolor, acrylic, pastel and pencil about the cycles that shape a life, made as the artist entered perimenopause and lost a monthly rhythm, and about the guides, symbols and bodies met along the way. Supported by a 4Culture grant.
shows.reception: First Thursday, October 1, 5-8pm; artist meet & greet Saturday, October 17, 1-3pm

shows.title: First Rain
shows.description: The gallery's third solo show by collage artist, printmaker and North Seattle College teacher Kelda Martensen. The new woodblock monotypes, built up through printmaking and collage, take their title from the relief that animals, plants, people and streets feel when rain comes after a long drought; her recurring water-drop shapes stand for tears, rain and waterways in landscapes that are both ecological and emotional.
shows.reception: First Thursday, November 5, 5-8pm (preview Saturday, October 31, 12-2pm; artist talk Saturday, November 14 at 1pm)

shows.title: Past Forward
shows.description: An exhibition of new work by Anne Hirondelle. The gallery has announced the title, dates and opening reception; no further text is posted yet.

shows.title: I Contain My Outside
shows.description: Intimate, interactive sculptures by Mia Mulvey, an artist and studio art professor whose work joins art, science, ceramics and technology. The pieces treat landscape as a store of memory and use unusual sound devices, including paper speakers and conductive, resonant sculptural forms, so that sound comes out of the material itself. The gallery recommends making an appointment to visit.
shows.reception: Opened Friday, September 11; artist talk Friday, November 6, 7pm; youth and family workshop Saturday, November 7, 2-4pm

shows.title: I will carry you over on my back: 2026 Fall MFA Show
shows.artist: Jayden Dukes, Gaeun Kim, Cameron McGaff, Skye Amber O'Brien
shows.description: The UW School of Art's annual fall MFA show brings together four graduate artists, Jayden Dukes, Gaeun Kim, Cameron McGaff and Skye Amber O'Brien, in performance, installation, sound art and found-object sculpture. The show reflects on accumulation, the underground, labor and capacity, and how systems and objects move toward loss, disrepair and failure. A free publication with a commissioned essay by Troy Sherman accompanies it.

shows.title: The Simple Cup Show
shows.description: KOBO's annual show celebrating the simple cup, co-curated with Seward Park Clay Studio, in which invited ceramic artists from North America and abroad each make their own take on the cup. The show opens with an in-person lottery for the chance to buy a cup, after which the cups are sold in the gallery and online until the show closes on December 24.

shows.title: Dwelling in the Light
shows.description: Seattle native Lisa Snow Lady shows acrylic paintings and layered paper collages that find beauty in everyday places. In bright colors she paints botanical gardens and lily ponds, flowers on tabletops, houses and Pacific Northwest scenes.
shows.reception: First Thursday Art Walk, October 1, 5-8pm; artist reception Second Saturday, October 10, 2-4pm

venue.address: 312 S Washington St, Seattle, WA 98104, USA

shows.title: Mouseness
shows.description:
Seattle artist Eunsun Choi fills METHOD's floor with Mouseness, a colony of small glowing robotic mice that wander the room and react to visitors. Each mouse carries sensors for people, light and nearby objects, and the project was developed over several years with electrical and computer engineering students at the University of Washington, where Choi is a DXARTS doctoral student.

METHOD shows immersive, site-specific installations; this run includes an Art Walk opening on October 1 and a panel discussion on October 17. The photos show the robots themselves from the artist's own documentation of the piece.
shows.reception: Thursday, October 1, 5-8pm (Art Walk); panel discussion Saturday, October 17, 2pm

shows.title: A Time of Change
shows.description: A group exhibition by members of Onyx Fine Arts Collective, the Pacific Northwest's longest-running community of artists of the African diaspora, at its Gallery Onyx space in Pacific Place. The featured image is Huey, a black-and-white portrait painting by Rasun Williams Jr. The September reception included live painting by abstract painter Sydney Noland and portrait painter Whitney Diggs.

shows.title: Emblematic
shows.description: Orcas Paley's eighth annual group show brings together 43 artists around the emblem as a way of making meaning, from badges, medals and seals to Renaissance emblem books. Works include gouache paintings, stained glass, collage, porcelain talismans, letterpress prints, wire and clay pieces, all small-scale and for sale.

shows.title: Bending Notes
shows.description: Paintings, assemblages and sculpture by Terry Turrell, a painter, sculptor and longtime singer-songwriter whose art is his way of making sense of the world. He builds with found materials such as jar lids, scrap metal, branches, peeling paint, wire, paper and fabric, and his sculptural work now runs through the construction of his oil and enamel paintings.
shows.reception: Saturday, October 3, 3-5pm (Q&A with the artist at 3:30pm)

shows.title: Wanderlust
shows.description: The gallery's first solo exhibition with Victoria Adams, who paints imagined panoramic landscapes with low horizons, glowing skies, open land, trees and still water. Working from memory, photographic details and the tradition of Western landscape painting, she makes scenes empty of people that suggest the pull of distant horizons.

shows.title: New Works
shows.description: New paintings by Ryan Molenkamp. The gallery has announced the dates and reception and says images of the show will be posted in early January.

shows.title: Hide & Seek
shows.description: A group show of functional, wearable masks by about a dozen artists, timed for Halloween: mythical monsters, curious creatures and demons you can wear. The masks are for sale, so visitors can pick one to finish a costume.

venue.address: 2000 NW Market St, Seattle, WA 98107, USA

shows.dates_note: Post gives only the October 10 opening; no closing date is posted (Push/Pull shows usually run about a month).

shows.title: Asakura Mitsuko: Eight Views
shows.description:
SAM has commissioned the Kyoto tapestry artist Asakura Mitsuko (born 1950) to weave Eight Views, a series of eight tapestries for the Garden Court at the center of the Seattle Asian Art Museum's 1933 Art Deco building. They will hang with other works from her more than fifty-year career.

The title refers to the East Asian tradition of the Eight Views, landscape poems and paintings traced to the 11th-century Chinese official Song Di and later carried to Japan, where Lake Biwa near Kyoto acquired its own Eight Views. Asakura grew up among Kyoto's kimono makers and Nishijin weavers and studied European tapestry in Amsterdam and Italy. The first image is Inspire (2007); the others show recent work by the artist from Salon 94, as the museum has not posted images of the new tapestries yet.

shows.title: Divine Disruption: The Art of Tsherin Sherpa
shows.description:

Trained in thangka painting, Sherpa brings the deities and spirits of Himalayan Buddhist art into the present, imagining how they might fare as migrants, adapting to new places alongside the Himalayan people.

More than twenty works, paintings, sculptures and a carpet, include well-known pieces that established his reputation and new works shown publicly for the first time, among them the bubble-gum-blowing figure Skipper Rising (2023), Himalayan Spirits (2021) and Spiritual Warrior (2020). shows.title: Freedom of Expression
shows.artist: Onyx Fine Arts Collective: Josiane Faubert, Angelena McQuarter, Sydney Noland, Angelika Grant and others
shows.description:
Freedom of Expression is a rotating exhibition in the Northwest African American Museum's Community Living Room, with work by artists of African descent living in the Pacific Northwest, supplied through the Onyx Fine Arts Collective. The museum presents it as a challenge to the idea that Black art is only "ethnic" art, and as a showing of the range of work these artists make.

The current rotation includes Josiane Faubert's oil painting Half Here, Half Somewhere, Angelena McQuarter's mixed-media Textile 2, Sydney Noland's Untitled (Stars) in enamel and oil pastel, Angelika Grant's acrylic Destiny, Juion Mitchell's mixed-media The Grass is Greener, Di Faria's fused glass The Watcher, and Entwined by 17-year-old Timberline High School student Nova Thomas. Faubert paints interiors as emotional landscapes drawn from her life between Gabon, France and the United States; Noland's star forms began as paper cutouts; Mitchell made many of his paintings inside his car.

shows.title: Making a Way: Jacob Lawrence
shows.description:
Making a Way: Jacob Lawrence and the Northwest Black Experience is an exhibition of works by Jacob Lawrence in the Northwest African American Museum's Journey Gallery. Through a series of his paintings and prints it looks at Black history, including in the Northwest, as Lawrence saw it.

Lawrence called his style "dynamic cubism". He drew on everyday life in Harlem, and by age 23 had finished five narrative series on figures and events in Black history, including Toussaint L'Ouverture, Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman. His work uses descriptive titles, flat blocks of color and simplified, angular figures, applied to subjects from neighborhood life and Black industrial labor to the Civil Rights Movement. He taught for 16 years as a professor at the University of Washington. The museum lists the show among its current exhibits but gives no dates.

shows.title: UNBLACKABLE
shows.description:
UNBLACKABLE is an exhibition of work by Seattle sports and entertainment artist TR Miles at the Northwest African American Museum, subtitled "Cannot be erased. Cannot be reduced. Cannot be undone." It treats Black presence, creativity, memory and self-determination, acknowledging displacement, suppression and racial violence without letting them define Black life as a whole.

Fragments are the show's central motif, and they match Miles's technique. He calls himself an abstract realist and works in two styles he named Broken Glass Art, in which a recognizable figure is built from many shards of color, and Pixel Painting, drawn freehand with a computer mouse. The installation pairs portraits of athletes, musicians and historical figures, among them Frederick Douglass and a jazz trumpeter, with wall texts on themes such as "The Impetus of the Cause Yet Resolved" and "To the Beat Y'all", and a wall asking visitors what UNBLACKABLE means to them.

shows.title: Ginny Ruffner: Project Aurora
shows.description:
Project Aurora is a permanent light installation by the Seattle artist Ginny Ruffner (1952-2025) at the National Nordic Museum. It is a wall of light 20 feet high and 10 feet wide made of 34,560 LEDs, across which sheets of colored light drawn from images of the aurora borealis ripple and drift. Microprocessors refresh the piece 20 times a second, and artificial intelligence gives the movement the unpredictability of the real aurora.

Ruffner made the work with video game developer Ed Fries and University of Washington lecturer Wanda Gregory. Best known for her glass sculpture, held in more than 50 museum collections, she turned to augmented reality and light in her later work. The installation runs Tuesday through Sunday from 3 to 11 pm and is included with general admission.

The ongoing series studies the commercial fishing industry through still lifes of the gear itself, found where it lies: rusted and cork floats, coiled rope and braided line, anchor chain, netting and buoys, photographed close up so they fill the frame.

The first pictures were made in 2025 at Seattle's Fishermen's Terminal and Squalicum Harbor in Bellingham; for this show they are joined by new photographs taken in summer 2026 aboard a Trident Seafoods boat in Alaska, a trip arranged by the museum. It runs alongside the museum's history exhibition A Ballard Story: Pacific Fishermen.

shows.title: Boundless: Stories of Asian Art
shows.description:
The long-term collection presentation that fills the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, installed when the 1933 Art Deco building reopened after its renovation in February 2020. Instead of galleries labeled by country, works from many cultures and periods are grouped around twelve themes central to Asian arts and societies, such as worship and celebration, visual arts and literature, and clothing and identity.

The south galleries hold art inspired by spiritual life (Awakened Ones, Bringing Blessings, The Divine Body) and the north galleries art inspired by material life (What is Precious?, Fashioning Eternity and others). From 2026 to 2031, works on long-term loan from the Rubin Museum of Himalayan Art join SAM's collection here. The images show the Dragon Tamer Luohan and other Chinese and Japanese highlights of the collection, then a gallery view.

shows.title: Ai Weiwei: Circle of Animals/Zodiac Heads
shows.description:
Ai Weiwei's Circle of Animals/Zodiac Heads (2010) is installed in the Ackerly Meadow just outside the PACCAR Pavilion at the Olympic Sculpture Park. The work is twelve cast-bronze animal heads, each more than ten feet tall and over 1,500 pounds, set in an arc in the order of the Chinese zodiac: Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Ram, Monkey, Rooster, Dog and Boar.

The heads reconceive the zodiac waterspouts of an 18th-century water-clock fountain at the Yuanmingyuan in Beijing, looted by British and French troops in 1860. Seven are based on surviving originals; Ai reimagined the five still missing. The park is free and open daily. The first image is a close-up of the Dog head; the second is the Seattle installation.

shows.title: American Art: The Stories We Carry
shows.description:
SAM's rehang of its third-floor American art galleries, made with SAM curators, staff, contemporary artists and community advisors and funded mainly by the Mellon Foundation and the Terra Foundation for American Art. Portraits, landscapes, sculpture, decorative arts and textiles from the historical collection are shown with new works and curation by contemporary artists, around themes of land and place, trade and migration, and the many American identities.

New commissions include Wendy Red Star's illuminated group portrait Áakiiwilaxpaake (People of the Earth) (2022). The other images are highlights of SAM's American collection: Albert Bierstadt's Puget Sound on the Pacific Coast, Sanford Gifford's Mount Rainier, Bay of Tacoma, John Singleton Copley's Dr. Silvester Gardiner, Raphaelle Peale's still life and Frederic Church's A Country Home. shows.title: Ash-Glazed Ceramics from Korea and Japan
shows.description:
Thirty-four ceramics with ash glaze, all from SAM's holdings of Japanese and Korean art, in the third-floor galleries. The selection runs from ancient Korean funerary and ritual gray wares and ancient Japanese Sue and Sanage wares to early medieval Japanese Seto wares and large storage jars from medieval and contemporary Japan.

The show explains how potters from the southern Korean peninsula brought the wheel and the anagama, a hillside kiln firing at 1,200 to 1,400 degrees centigrade, to Japan in the Kofun period. In those kilns wood ash settling on the pots produced natural, or accidental, glazes ranging from greenish yellow to deep green, sandy to glossy. Organized by the Seattle Art Museum. Images after the first three come from SAM's online collection records that describe ash glaze; the museum's page names only the first three.

shows.title: Diego Cibelli: Fiori dei Miei Habiti / La Montagne Enchantée
shows.description:
In SAM's Porcelain Room on the fourth floor, the Neapolitan artist Diego Cibelli presents porcelain sculpture made in response to the room's ceiling fresco, The Triumph of Valor over Time (ca. 1757) by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, an allegory in which Victory crowns Valor while Time watches from the shadows.

Cibelli's centerpiece is a mountainous white peak down which human figures tumble, their bodies turning into branches, leaves and flowers as they fall, a return to nature; smaller pieces, including a goat-headed figure, surround it. Cibelli works closely with the historic Capodimonte porcelain manufactory in Naples. The project is guest curated by Christian Larsen. The last image is a view of the installation in the Porcelain Room.

shows.title: DRIFT: Meadow
shows.description:
Meadow is a kinetic installation by DRIFT, the Netherlands studio founded in 2007 by Lonneke Gordijn and Ralph Nauta. An inverted field of large mechanical flowers made of fabric, aluminum and LEDs hangs high overhead; the blossoms open and close in response to the people below, who take the place of the sun. The flower colors are chosen from local flora, so each installation is specific to its site.

DRIFT's sculptures and performances are meant to reconnect viewers with natural processes. SAM lists the run as Nov 16, 2026 to Apr 11, 2027, and its page notes the installation is temporarily closed due to construction. The image is SAM's own installation view.

shows.title: FriendsWithYou: Little Cloud Sky
shows.artist: FriendsWithYou (Samuel Borkson and Arturo Sandoval III)
shows.description:
Little Cloud Sky (2025) is a SAM commission from FriendsWithYou, the Los Angeles duo Samuel Borkson and Arturo Sandoval III. Forty of their signature Little Cloud characters, each four feet wide and molded in thermoplastic, hang from the ceiling of the Brotman Forum, the museum's main entrance lobby, which is free to enter without a ticket.

Versions of the skyscape have appeared in Las Vegas, Miami, Tokyo and London, but this is a new iteration and the artists' first long-term museum installation. The Little Cloud is a recurring figure in their work, meant as a symbol of peace and connection. The images show the Little Cloud character and the clouds in SAM's lobby; the commission was organized by José Carlos Diaz.

shows.title: SAM on Paper: Goya's Los Caprichos
shows.description:
A selection from Francisco de Goya's Los Caprichos is on view in SAM's European galleries. Goya published the series of eighty etchings in 1799, aiming sardonic and often surreal scenes at Spanish society at the end of the 18th century: superstition, the Inquisition, the decadence of the ruling classes and the hypocrisy of the status quo, set against Enlightenment ideas of reason and reform. Captions added by Goya hint at each image's meaning.

Goya gave the copper plates to the Royal Chalcography in Madrid in 1803. SAM's prints come from the tenth edition, printed from the original plates between 1910 and 1928. The images here are plates from SAM's set as shown in its online collection; the museum does not list which plates are currently hung.

shows.title: Impressionisms: The Global Nineteenth Century
shows.description:
A fourth-floor gallery of European and American painting from the long 19th century, from the French Revolution to the First World War, drawn from SAM's collection. It traces artists who loosened academic conventions and, working in networks across the Atlantic, painted landscapes, city streets and domestic interiors in the loose manner called Impressionism.

The wall text names Childe Hassam and Willard Metcalf, Lucien Pissarro and Claude Monet in the countryside and city; Gustave Caillebotte, Mary Cassatt, Vilhelm Hammershøi and Berthe Morisot in private interiors; and William Merritt Chase and Victoria Dubourg in still life. Images show SAM's works by these artists; the museum does not publish a full checklist.

shows.title: Lessons from the Institute of Empathy
shows.description:
In SAM's fourth-floor African art galleries, Saya Woolfalk's ChimaTEK: Virtual Chimeric Space (2015-16) is installed among works from the museum's African collection. Three of Woolfalk's Empathics, costumed hybrid figures, preside over an immersive space where visitors are invited to step outside their routine selves and practice understanding others.

The work was first shown in SAM's 2015 exhibition Disguise: Masks and Global African Art and is now in the permanent collection. Around it are masks, jewelry and garments presented as lessons in empathy, including a Soundsuit by Nick Cave. The installation, on view since 2018, closes November 29, 2026. The last image shows one of the gallery's lesson cases.

shows.title: Chris Kallmyer: Song Cycle
shows.description:
Song Cycle (2021) is a kinetic sculpture by the musician and artist Chris Kallmyer: a 256-character split-flap sign, like the arrival and departure boards of 20th-century airports and train stations, that continually spells out and rewrites fragments of poetry, part imagined, part remembered and part observed. Originally commissioned by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, it hangs in SAM's Brotman Forum, the free entrance lobby, as a bridge between the public space and the galleries.

Kallmyer, a CalArts graduate and longtime collaborator with the new-music collective Wild Up, has made projects for SFMOMA, the Walker Art Center, the Getty and LACMA. SAM's page currently notes the work is temporarily closed due to construction.

shows.title: Karon Davis: Not My Circus
shows.description:
The solo exhibition of Karon Davis, winner of the 2025 Gwendolyn Knight and Jacob Lawrence Prize, in SAM's third-floor galleries. Davis, a Los Angeles artist born in 1977, makes life-size figures from plaster casts of real people, then builds them out with glass eyes, chicken wire and found objects into tableaux between sculpture and performance.

Not My Circus turns the gallery into a big top: a lion subdued by a greater force, a weeping clown, a knife-thrower's assistant, and other circus roles that stand in for the power dynamics of wider society. Curated by Carrie Dedon. The first image is Sad Clown (2025) from the show; the others are recent works by the artist from Salon 94, as SAM has not posted more of the new pieces yet.

shows.title: Monochrome: Calder and Tara Donovan
shows.description:
The third exhibition in SAM's multi-year Calder at SAM initiative pairs the sculptor and installation artist Tara Donovan with Alexander Calder. Donovan chose two of Calder's black works as touchpoints: the large hanging mobile Jacaranda (1949) and the stabile Mountains (1:5 intermediate maquette, 1976) from SAM's own collection.

Around them are works from several of Donovan's series, each made from a single mass-produced material: a floor installation of layered tar paper (Transplanted), a wall work built from Slinky toys, framed works, and a room-filling cluster of Mylar and hot glue. The show treats monochrome as a way of drawing attention to material, light and movement. The images show Donovan's Mylar work (detail), Calder's Jacaranda, Transplanted (detail) and, last, a view of the SAM installation.

shows.title: Qiu Zhijie: Map of the History of Science and Technology
shows.description:
In the PACCAR Pavilion at the Olympic Sculpture Park, the Chinese artist Qiu Zhijie (born 1969) presents an ink-on-paper wall map designed for the park. The Map of the History of Science and Technology turns scientific and technical advances from Asia and the West, from ancient to contemporary times, into an imaginary landscape of mountains, lakes and rivers: the discovery of bronze and iron, the wheel, the abacus, the plow, celadon ware, Roman cement, papermaking, the bicycle, photography, acupuncture and the flush toilet among them.

Qiu, trained in traditional calligraphy and a leading figure in Chinese conceptual and new-media art, is known for these memory-palace maps. He is President of the Tianjin Academy of Fine Arts. The pavilion is free to enter.

shows.title: A Room for Animal Intelligence
shows.description:
A fourth-floor installation of about one hundred animal images drawn from across SAM's collection, presented as if the animals themselves were addressing visitors about what they see happening on the planet. Pets, livestock, birds, insects and predators appear side by side, from a Coast Salish mosquito mask by Francis Horne Sr. (1999) to Egyptian bronzes, Japanese netsuke, ancient Greek and Chinese figures and an American Art Deco bronze of playing greyhounds.

Wall texts are written in the animals' voices, and the gallery includes oversized animal figures among the objects. The museum's online collection lists the works in the room under the exhibition's name; the images here are drawn from that list.

shows.title: The Surrealist International: Fifty Years of Dreams
shows.artist: Dorothea Tanning, Salvador Dalí, René Magritte, Joan Miró, Leonora Carrington and others
shows.description:
A touring exhibition drawn from Tate's collection that follows Surrealism from the 1920s to the 1970s and around the world, presented in collaboration with Tate. Paintings, sculpture, photographs and archival material treat Surrealism as a state of mind taken up by individuals and groups in many places.

Well-known artists such as Louise Bourgeois, Leonora Carrington, Salvador Dalí, René Magritte, Joan Miró and Dorothea Tanning appear alongside lesser-known figures including Ithell Colquhoun, Kati Horna, Malangatana Ngwenya, Osamu Shiihara and Lionel Wendt. The show marks the centenary of the first Surrealist exhibition in Paris in 1925. Images after Tanning's Eine Kleine Nachtmusik come from the tour's 2026 stop at the Frist Art Museum, Nashville, where the same Tate loans were shown.

shows.title: Yirrkala: Art from Australia’s Top End
shows.description:
A third-floor gallery of art from Yirrkala, the Aboriginal community in northeast Arnhem Land on Australia's north coast. Artists there paint sacred clan designs with local earth pigments on stringybark (eucalyptus) bark, and more recently on discarded metal transformed into fields of shimmering pattern. Diamond shapes may stand for fire, honey or the churning water around a diving crocodile.

The presentation centers on environmental cycles and the ancestral powers in land and water, opening with Gunybi Ganambarr's Mundukul at Baraltja (2008), a promised gift of Margaret Levi and Robert Kaplan. Moving-image works by Yirrkala's media artists are also shown. The images show the Ganambarr painting (detail), a bark painting by Wolpa Wanambi and a larrakitj memorial pole by Wanyubi Marika from SAM's collection, and a view of the gallery.

shows.title: DISplace
shows.description:
DISplace looks at the people and histories that connect Hawaiʻi and the Pacific Northwest, starting with the first documented Native Hawaiians to reach the West Coast in 1787. It is co-curated by Native Hawaiian artist and kapa maker Lehuauakea and Portland artist and educator Kanani Miyamoto, both of the mixed-Native Hawaiian diaspora. The title reads as "dis place", this place.

The show combines art by eleven regional Native Hawaiian artists with family stories and ephemera, historic photographs and archival objects. The artists are Keliko K. M. Adams, Haʻaheo Auwae-Dekker, Daphne Kauahiʻilani Jenkins, Nyomi Iwalani José, Lōkela Alexander Minami, Brandon Naihe, Malia Peoples, Cris Romento, Shaka Funk Design Co., Mikiʻala Souza and Bruce Clayton Tom; works include Souza's monotype Guidelines, Minami's painting of a voyaging canoe at the Seattle waterfront, woven wall hangings and Naihe's leaf print.

shows.title: Desire to Make: The Art of Kikuko Dewa
shows.description:
Desire to Make: The Art of Kikuko Dewa is an upcoming Wing Luke Museum exhibition on the Japanese American artist Kikuko Dewa (1933-2010), covering her textiles, fashion and inventive working processes and the relationships that shaped her work. It is curated by Michelle Kumata, the Seattle artist and former Wing Luke exhibit director, and includes contributing artists Junko Yamamoto, Akiko Sato, Yoko Nomura and Lorraine Pai.

Dewa came from a family of weavers in Kyoto's Nishijin district. After moving to the United States she worked as a seamstress for Seattle clothing companies, later ran her own clothing design business in Greenwood that often used antique kimono silks, and for about twenty years taught shibori dyeing at the Cherry Blossom Festival. Her work was shown at the Seattle Art Museum and the Wing Luke Asian Museum. The image is a detail of a textile by Dewa from the museum's announcement; the museum has not posted further images yet.

The fifteen artists are J. D. (2024), Kyler Pahang's oil painting A Cry for Uran (2024), and Hilary Lee's digital images of food. The exhibition has been extended to February 14, 2027.

The Sky Is a Diasporic Space is the latest exhibition by YouthCAN, the Wing Luke Museum's free arts and mentorship program for high school students, installed in the museum's Frank Fujii Youth Gallery. It looks at collective memory and who gets remembered, made in response to attacks on migrant communities while the students studied how art has supported solidarity movements around the world.

The show includes block prints, kites, oral histories and personal mementos. Hand-printed placemats on burlap, made by several students with teaching artist Saiyare Refaei, stand for "extending our table" and invite visitors to sit in the gallery. A filing cabinet time capsule holds collages of the students' current interests, photos of friends, oral histories recorded with students from UW Bothell's Southeast Asian Pasts and Futures program, and news clippings, and visitors may browse its folders. The teaching artists were Spur Lowe, Saiyare Refaei and JM Wong, with 350 Seattle.

It centers the knowledge of Black and Brown women and femmes and asks visitors to sit, listen and think about who kept them and what worlds they are building.
